PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 78 — Lesson 102: Stroke & TIA Management

FNP-level goal: Treat sudden focal neurologic symptoms as a time-sensitive emergency, distinguish transient symptoms from benign symptoms only after appropriate evaluation, organize etiologic secondary prevention, and support safe functional recovery after stroke.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, transient ischemic attack, seizure, migraine, hypoglycemia, and other stroke mimics require a rapid, safety-first approach.
  • Recognize high-risk sudden focal symptoms and activate emergency care even when symptoms resolve before the visit.
  • Use a focused history, neurologic examination, medication review, and functional assessment without delaying definitive emergency imaging or treatment.
  • Connect stroke mechanism to secondary prevention: blood pressure, lipid management, diabetes, tobacco, atrial fibrillation, carotid disease, antithrombotics, and rehabilitation.
  • Apply FNP scope boundaries for anticoagulation, antiplatelet treatment, post-discharge reconciliation, depression screening, swallowing safety, caregiver support, and specialist coordination.

Part 1 — Stroke Is a Brain Emergency

Stroke is a clinical syndrome caused by interrupted blood flow or bleeding in the brain. Ischemic stroke results from arterial occlusion; hemorrhagic stroke results from bleeding. Both can produce sudden focal deficits and both require rapid emergency differentiation because treatment pathways diverge. A transient ischemic attack is a transient neurologic dysfunction caused by focal ischemia without acute infarction on imaging, but in real time it cannot be safely distinguished from a completed stroke by symptom duration alone.

The FNP's first job is not to localize every lesion perfectly. It is to recognize a possible time-sensitive brain event, determine the last known well time, identify immediate threats, activate emergency medical services, and avoid delays caused by a lengthy outpatient workup.

Part 2 — Think BE FAST, Then Think Beyond It

Balance change, eye or visual symptoms, facial droop, arm or leg weakness or numbness, speech or language difficulty, and time to call emergency services are useful public-facing prompts. But posterior circulation events may present with sudden severe imbalance, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, or vomiting; cortical events may present with neglect, aphasia, visual field loss, or confusion. Sudden focal symptoms should be treated as stroke until proven otherwise, even if the patient is young, has a normal blood pressure, or looks improved when evaluated.

Ask the exact last known well time, not merely when the patient noticed symptoms. Ask who witnessed onset, whether symptoms were abrupt or progressive, anticoagulant use, recent surgery or bleeding, seizure activity, glucose status when available without delaying transfer, trauma, headache, neck pain, pregnancy or postpartum status, and baseline function. Document the time and what the patient or witness reports; do not imply certainty that is not present.

Part 3 — TIA Is a Warning, Not a Reassurance

Transient unilateral weakness, aphasia, monocular visual loss, or other focal deficit that resolves can be a TIA. Resolution does not make the event harmless. Early recurrent stroke risk can be substantial, and the patient needs urgent evaluation to identify a mechanism and prevent recurrence. A patient who says the arm weakness lasted ten minutes and is now normal should not be scheduled for a routine office visit next month.

Transient symptoms can also result from seizure with postictal deficit, migraine aura, hypoglycemia, medication effect, functional neurologic disorder, peripheral nerve compression, or metabolic illness. These possibilities do not justify dismissing a high-risk focal episode before emergency assessment. A mimic diagnosis is often made after, not before, appropriate acute evaluation.

Part 4 — Focused Examination Without Delaying Transfer

In a patient already being transferred, perform only the assessment that improves immediate safety and handoff: airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs, glucose if quickly available, mental status, facial symmetry, speech and language, visual complaint, gaze, motor drift, sensory asymmetry, coordination, gait only if safe, and signs of trauma. Note anticoagulants, insulin or hypoglycemic agents, blood pressure medicines, and last known well. Do not let an extended outpatient neurologic exam or scheduling an office MRI delay emergency imaging and stroke-team evaluation.

In post-discharge follow-up, reassess residual deficits, mobility, falls, swallowing and aspiration risk, speech, vision, cognition, mood, sleep, bowel and bladder function, caregiver strain, medication understanding, and access to rehabilitation. Stroke recovery is not only motor recovery; hidden cognitive, emotional, communication, and social deficits determine whether a plan is safe.

Part 5 — Mechanism Determines Prevention

Secondary prevention is not one-size-fits-all. Large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism such as atrial fibrillation, small-vessel disease, carotid stenosis, arterial dissection, hypercoagulability, and less common mechanisms have different management implications. After an ischemic event, the FNP should obtain the hospital summary, brain and vascular imaging interpretation, echocardiography or rhythm-monitoring results when relevant, antithrombotic plan, and specific follow-up recommendations. Do not guess the mechanism based only on age or risk factors.

For most patients with ischemic stroke or TIA without contraindication, an antithrombotic strategy is part of secondary prevention. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy have different indications. Long-term dual antiplatelet therapy is not routine for all patients, and combining anticoagulation with antiplatelets is usually not appropriate unless a specific indication exists. The duration and choice must follow the stroke mechanism, bleeding risk, and the discharging neurology or cardiology plan.

Part 6 — Atrial Fibrillation and Cardioembolic Risk

Atrial fibrillation can cause atrial stasis, thrombus formation, and embolic stroke. New AF, irregular pulse, or palpitations may require ECG and risk-based evaluation, but a normal single ECG does not necessarily exclude intermittent AF. After cryptogenic stroke, prolonged rhythm monitoring may be pursued by the stroke team. Anticoagulation decisions should account for stroke mechanism, bleeding risk, kidney function, weight or dosing criteria when relevant, drug interactions, adherence, affordability, fall risk in context, and whether a mechanical valve or significant mitral stenosis changes the treatment pathway.

Never stop, start, bridge, or combine anticoagulants casually after stroke. In the outpatient setting, verify the exact drug, dose, timing, renal monitoring, procedure plan, and prescriber responsible for each decision. New severe headache, neurologic symptoms, significant bleeding, head injury, or melena while anticoagulated may require urgent evaluation.

Part 7 — Vascular Risk Reduction Is Brain Protection

Blood pressure control, lipid-lowering therapy, diabetes management, tobacco cessation, physical activity within rehabilitation and safety limits, nutrition, sleep-apnea assessment when indicated, medication adherence, and reduction of harmful alcohol or stimulant exposure are core components of secondary prevention. The target and medication plan should be individualized after review of the event subtype, imaging, kidney function, orthostasis, fall risk, and specialist plan. A patient with a recent stroke may have treatment goals different from a patient without vascular disease.

Carotid disease is a specific, time-sensitive example. Severe symptomatic extracranial carotid stenosis may warrant early procedural evaluation in selected patients, while other patients need medical therapy alone. The FNP must promptly obtain and communicate imaging results and specialty recommendations rather than promise a procedure or assume carotid stenosis is the cause of every event.

Part 8 — Rehabilitation Is Secondary Prevention Too

Early and ongoing rehabilitation can improve function and prevent complications. Coordinate physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, swallowing evaluation, vision rehabilitation, cognitive care, fall prevention, adaptive devices, driving assessment when needed, and caregiver training. Screen for post-stroke depression, anxiety, fatigue, sleep disturbance, pain, spasticity, and social isolation. A patient who can walk into clinic may still be unable to manage medications, work safely, cook, drive, communicate needs, or return to an unsafe home environment.

Use a functional question set: What has changed in eating, bathing, transfers, walking, stairs, toileting, medication management, finances, driving, work, language, memory, and mood? Convert answers into actionable referrals, caregiver supports, and follow-up dates.

Part 9 — FNP Case: Symptoms Resolved Before Arrival

A 63-year-old reports ten minutes of expressive aphasia and right hand weakness that fully resolved while waiting for the appointment. The FNP determines the last known well time, checks stability and glucose without delay, activates emergency evaluation, and communicates that this may be a TIA or stroke. Resolution is a warning, not a reason to wait for an outpatient MRI.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Post-Stroke Medication List

A patient returns after ischemic stroke with aspirin, an anticoagulant, two statins listed in different systems, and unclear instructions. The FNP obtains the discharge summary and pharmacy fill history, verifies the stroke mechanism and intended antithrombotic plan with the responsible team, reconciles duplication, reviews bleeding precautions, and ensures neurology follow-up is scheduled. Safe reconciliation is a therapeutic intervention.

Part 11 — FNP Case: A Hidden Recovery Barrier

A patient with minor facial weakness appears physically improved but misses medications and appointments. The partner reports word-finding problems and forgetfulness. The FNP screens cognition, medication management ability, mood, and caregiver strain; engages speech or occupational therapy and social support; and adjusts the care plan. A low NIHSS at discharge does not guarantee independent self-management.

FNP High-Yield Framework: TIME

  1. T — Time last known well: document onset history and activate emergency pathways promptly.
  2. I — Identify focal deficits and instability: sudden weakness, language, vision, balance, severe headache, altered consciousness, or airway risk are emergencies.
  3. M — Mechanism guides maintenance: obtain imaging, rhythm, vascular, and discharge data before changing antithrombotics.
  4. E — Enable recovery: rehabilitation, swallowing, cognition, mood, falls, caregiver support, access, and closed-loop specialty follow-up.

Take-Home Summary

Stroke and TIA management begins with speed and continues with mechanism-specific prevention and functional recovery. A transient focal deficit may be an emergency even when the patient looks normal in clinic. After discharge, the FNP prevents recurrence by reconciling complex plans, controlling vascular risk, recognizing anticoagulant and antiplatelet boundaries, and addressing the cognitive, emotional, and social work of recovery.

Educational note: This lesson supports FNP clinical reasoning and does not replace emergency stroke protocols, neurologic assessment, current antithrombotic guidance, imaging interpretation, or specialist consultation. Sudden focal neurologic symptoms, severe acute headache, altered consciousness, or new neurologic deficit requires emergency evaluation.
